clues: A boat-shaped bone in the proximal wrist row.
It has a retrograde blood supply that puts its proximal part at risk.
It is the carpal bone most often fractured after falling onto an outstretched hand.
A prominent bony process at the proximal end of a forearm bone.
It enters a fossa on the posterior humerus during elbow extension.
It forms the tip of the elbow where triceps brachii inserts.
A broad muscle arising from slips on the lateral chest wall.
It protracts the scapula and holds its medial border against the ribs.
Long thoracic nerve injury paralyzes it, causing a winged scapula.
A major somatic nerve network serving the shoulder and upper limb.
It organizes fibers into roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and terminal branches.
It is formed by the anterior rami of C5 through T1.
A birth or traction palsy involving the upper part of the brachial plexus.
It affects nerves carrying C5 and C6 fibers.
It causes an adducted, medially rotated arm and extended forearm.
One of four muscles reinforcing the shoulder joint capsule.
It lies above the scapular spine and is supplied by the suprascapular nerve.
It initiates abduction of the arm at the glenohumeral joint.
An intermuscular gap in the posterior shoulder region.
It lies between teres minor, teres major, triceps long head, and surgical neck.
The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery pass through it.
A terminal nerve arising from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus.
It pierces coracobrachialis and continues as a forearm cutaneous nerve.
It innervates biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis.
A broad fibrous expansion originating from a major anterior arm muscle.
It crosses medially across the cubital fossa deep to superficial veins.
It helps shield the brachial artery and median nerve during venipuncture.
A deep motor nerve branch in the posterior forearm.
It emerges after piercing through the supinator muscle.
It supplies posterior forearm extensors and is the continuation of deep radial nerve.
A purely motor branch arising in the forearm from the median nerve.
It runs along the anterior interosseous membrane toward the wrist.
It innervates flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus, and lateral FDP.
A thick fibrous band on the palmar aspect of the wrist.
It bridges between the scaphoid/trapezium and pisiform/hook of hamate.
It forms the roof of the carpal tunnel.
A small triangular depression on the dorsolateral wrist when extending the thumb.
Its floor contains the radial artery and scaphoid bone.
It is bounded by tendons of abductor pollicis longus, EPB, and EPL.
A rounded muscular pad on the palmar hand.
It contains muscles that abduct, oppose, and flex the first digit.
It forms the fleshy prominence at the base of the thumb.
Four small worm-like intrinsic muscles of the hand.
They arise from flexor digitorum profundus tendons and join extensor expansions.
They flex MCP joints while extending interphalangeal joints of the fingers.
An intrinsic hand muscle with oblique and transverse heads.
It is supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
It draws the thumb toward the palm and index finger.
A ring-like structure attached around a shallow articular socket.
It is composed of fibrocartilage rather than hyaline articular cartilage.
It deepens the glenoid cavity of the scapula.
A ring-like fibrous band near the elbow joint.
It attaches to the ulna around the proximal end of the radius.
It holds the radial head in the radial notch while allowing rotation.
A major superficial vein of the upper limb.
It runs along the deltopectoral groove before piercing the clavipectoral fascia.
It ascends on the lateral side of the forearm and arm to join the axillary vein.
A serious musculoskeletal complication in the anterior forearm.
It follows impaired arterial inflow and tissue ischemia after trauma.
It causes permanent flexion deformity and fibrosis after brachial artery injury.
